source_text:
LIBER PRIMUS
De S. S. Theologiae natura et constitutione.

CAPUT PRIMUM.
De Theologiae definitione.

Theologia est habitus intellectus practicus, e patefactione divina sacris scripturis mystico Spiritu S. plene consignata, hominem in via Spiritus pro aetate, vocatione et mensura fidei suae, docens rationem colendi DEO et consequendi vitam aeternam, ad DEI gloriam.

SCHOLION.
Principio hic quaeritur, quid significet proprie vox THEOLOGIA, an in sacra Scriptura legatur Theoloquium, Deiloquium, id est rationem vel orationem DEI, qua a DEO instituimur; aut rationem, vel orationem, vel conceptum mentis de DEO rebusque divinis e scripturis virtute Spiritus sancti efformatum: quo utroque sensu hic accipitur.

Nam gravissime B. Irenaeus: DEUM, inquit, vere agnoscere nemo potest, nisi DEO ipso docente; ex Joh. 6.45. Est scriptum in Prophetis, Et erunt omnes docti a DEO. Quisquis ergo audivit a Patre et didicit venit ad me. Non enim relictis est, ait Hilarius lib. 7. de Trin., hominum eloquiis de DEI rebus, aliis, praeterquam DEI sermo. Omnia reliqua et arcta et conclusa et impedita sunt et obscura. Si aliquis aliis verbis demonstrare hoc, quam quibus a DEO dictum est, volet: aut ipse non intelligit, aut legentibus non intelligendum relinquit. Ex lib. 1. de Trin.: Cum de rebus DEI sermo est, concedamus cognitionem sui DEO; dictioni ejus pia veneratione famulemur. Idoneus enim sibi testis est qui seipsum cognitus non est. Coeli mysterium, ait Ambrosius lib. 5. ep. 31., doceat me Deus ipse qui condidit, non homo qui seipsum ignoravit. Cui magis de DEO, quam DEO credam?

Ne tamen quis fanaticus dicto Christi Joh. 6.45. abutatur, hic digna considerata est ejus expositio, quam habet Urbanus Regius, praeteriti seculi gravis Theologus, in corpore doctrinae Julio de formulis caute loquendi sub titulo nono. Nos, inquiens, temere hunc locum produco. Nam ab imperitis jactatur tanquam encomium IMPERITIAE. Et hic putant se verbum DEI aet habere, quo OMNES BONAE ARTES et ipsa denique Theologiae studia explodantur. Christus satis explicat hunc locum Joh. 6. Nemo potest, inquit, venire ad me nisi Pater, qui misit me, traxerit eum, et ego resuscitabo eum in novissimo die. Et scriptum in prophetis: Et erunt omnes docti a DEO. Omnis ergo qui audivit a patre, et didicit, venit ad me. Hic Christus de COMMUNI illa et OMNIBUS SALVANDIS NECESSARIA doctrina loquitur; qua Christum agnoscimus esse Filium DEI propter nostram salutem hominem factum, et in eum, ut nostrum unicum Salvatorem, credimus. Hac doctrina illuminantur certe omnes electi: et qui ea carent, condemnabuntur: sed est etiam in ecclesia ALIA ERUDITIO, quae vocatur DONUM PROPHETIAE, quo dono donantur non omnes Christiani, sed qui Ecclesiis docendis praeficiuntur ut Scripturas sanctas exponant, ad aedificationem, exhortationem et consolationem, cujus mentio fit 1. Cor. 14. Hoc donum NON EST OMNIBUS CREDENTIBUS, SARTORIBUS et SUTORIBUS et Apostolis commune: quo qui carent, non debent docere in Ecclesia, sed docentes reverenter audire, ut Apostolus ait: Qui non est interpres, taceat in Ecclesia, ceterum sibi ipsi loquatur et Deo. Haec ibidem.

In scripturis quidem disertim non legitur vox Theologia praeter illius conjugatum in inscriptione Apocalypsis, ubi Johannes Euangelista Theologus dicitur; strictissimo significatu; qui asseruit divinitatem Logou tum historia Euangelica, tum Apocalypsi sua: frequentatur tamen tum a priscis patribus, tum a profanis scriptoribus, tum a scholasticis, tum denique a recentioribus Theologis. Neque opus est, ut vocabulum technicum in scripturis exstet; quia hae non formulas artium ac disciplinarum, sed res credendas ad salutem proponunt.
english: Book I. On the nature and constitution of sacred theology. Chapter 1. On the definition of theology.

Theology is a practical habit of the intellect, fully sealed by the mystical Holy Spirit from the divine disclosure in the Holy Scriptures, teaching a person on the Spirit's way — according to age, calling, and the measure of his own faith — the manner of worshipping God and of obtaining eternal life, unto the glory of God.

Scholion. First it is asked what the word theology properly signifies: whether in Holy Scripture one reads a God-speech or God-discourse — that is, the reason or speech of God by which we are instructed by God — or the reason, speech, or mental conception about God and divine things formed from the Scriptures by the power of the Holy Spirit. It is taken here in both senses.

For most weightily blessed Irenaeus says that no one can truly know God unless God himself teaches; from ([[John 6:45 >> Bible:John 6:45]]): It is written in the Prophets, And they shall all be taught by God. Whoever therefore has heard from the Father and has learned comes to me. For it is not left, says Hilary in book 7 On the Trinity, to human eloquence to speak of the things of God by other words than the speech of God. All other things are narrow, shut in, hindered, and obscure. If anyone wants to demonstrate this by other words than those by which it was spoken by God, either he himself does not understand, or he leaves it not to be understood by his readers. From book 1 On the Trinity: When the discourse is about the things of God, let us grant the knowledge of himself to God; let us serve his speech with pious reverence. For he is a fit witness for himself who is not known as to himself. Let the mystery of heaven, says Ambrose in book 5, letter 31, be taught me by God himself who made it, not by man who has not known himself. To whom should I rather trust concerning God than to God?

Yet lest some fanatic abuse Christ's saying in ([[John 6:45 >> Bible:John 6:45]]), here is worth considering the exposition which Urbanus Regius, a serious theologian of the past age, has in the body of doctrine to Julius on formulas for speaking carefully, under the ninth title. We, he says, do not rashly produce this place. For by the unskilled it is tossed about as an encomium of ignorance. And here they think they have a word of God by which all the liberal arts and even the studies of theology themselves may be exploded. Christ sufficiently explains this place in John 6: No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, and I will raise him up on the last day. And it is written in the prophets: And they shall all be taught by God. Everyone therefore who has heard from the Father and has learned comes to me. Here Christ speaks of that common doctrine necessary for all who are to be saved, by which we acknowledge Christ to be the Son of God made man for our salvation, and believe in him as our only Savior. By this doctrine certainly all the elect are illuminated; and those who lack it will be condemned. But there is also in the church another learning, which is called the gift of prophecy, with which gift not all Christians are endowed, but those who are set over churches for teaching, that they may expound the Holy Scriptures unto edification, exhortation, and consolation, of which mention is made in ([[1 Corinthians 14:1-5 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:1-5]]). This gift is not common to all believers — to tailors and cobblers and apostles alike. Those who lack it ought not to teach in the church, but reverently to hear those who teach, as the Apostle says: If there is no interpreter, let him keep silence in the church, and let him speak to himself and to God.

Indeed the word theology is not read expressly in the Scriptures except for its cognate in the title of the Apocalypse, where John the Evangelist is called Theologian in the strictest sense, as one who asserted the divinity of the Word both by the Gospel history and by his Apocalypse. Yet the term is frequented by the ancient fathers, by profane writers, by the schoolmen, and finally by more recent theologians. Nor is it necessary that a technical vocabulary exist in the Scriptures, because they do not propose the formulas of arts and disciplines, but the things to be believed unto salvation.

source_text: X. Quis FINIS sacrae Theologiae sit? 1. Finis sacrae Theologiae duplex consideratur, internus et externus; internus est mysteria et dogmata sacra e scripturis docere, hoc est, recte explicare, demonstrare ac defendere ad excitandam in auditoribus vitam Dei: externus est vita Dei, qua creatori, redemtori et sanctificatori nostro unimur, subjicimur et obedimus in luce, Ephe. 4.17.18. seu beatitudo hominis inchoata, quae est fidei, tum consummata quae est visionis sive vita aeterna, qua nos in via et patria in Deo bene est, eoque nutrimur roboramur et recreamur tanquam ultimo fine nostro reali personali, Gen. 15.1. 2. Vita haec una eademque quod ad essentiam, a suo principio permanet in aeternum, Joh. 3.36. cap. 5.24. 1. Joh. 3.15. 3. Est autem Deo vivere et Christo Rom. 6.10.11. et justitiae 1. Petr. 2.24. omnes nostras actiones et operationes fidei vitaeque secundum voluntatem Dei, ad gloriam Dei dirigere, eisque illis servire, Ipso Deo intus agente. 4. Sic dicimur secundum carnem vivere, Rom. 8.12.13. i.e. omnes nostras actiones ad libitum originalis malitiae instituere et peragere. Cui contrarium est spiritu vivere, Gal. 5.25. juste, sobrie, pie vivere, ad Titum 2.12. non amplius cupiditatibus hominum, sed voluntati Dei quod in carne reliquum est temporis vivere, et vivere secundum Deum, i.e. spiritu, 1. Pet. 4.v.2.6. Sic Paulus Gal. 2.v.19.20. ut Deo, inquit, vivam, una cum Christo crucifixus sum, i.e. mortificatus sum, sive vetus Adamus meus jugulatus est et novus in me conditus, ut Deo posthac spiritu novitatis serviam, 2. Cor. 4.v.10. et Phil. 1.v.20. 5. Vita DEI, non qua Deus ipse vivit, qui ipsissima vita est, sed qua nos ab eo vivificamur, vel potius vivimus, bifariam accipi potest, Eph. 4.18. vel quae censetur coram DEO, ut gloria DEI Joh. 12.43. justitia DEI, Rom. 10.3.4.6. per gratiam Euangelicae justificationis: vel quam Deus nobis communicat, per spiritum regenerationis. 6. Utrovis modo sumas, eadem tamen sententia est. Nam communis haec vita, qua sumus homines, ad vitam Dei comparata, nihil aliud est, quam inane simulacrum vitae, non modo quia cito praeterit, sed etiam quod animae nostrae vivendo mortuae sunt, cum Deo non adhaerent. 7. Occurrunt autem in hoc mundo quattuor vitae gradus. Nam una est communissima, quae duntaxat vigore constat, qui etiam in plantas ac regnum vegetabile competit et a Paracelsistis ad regnum minerale quoque exporrigitur. Altera universalis, quae motu et sensu constat, cujus etiam participes sunt bestiae. Quam Thomas Campanella libris de sensu rerum ad omnes mundi partes, partiumque particulas extendit. Tertia humana, qua sumus filii Adami. Quarta vero est supernaturalis, quam soli fideles obtinent. 8. Omnes hi vitae gradus a Deo sunt, ideoque vita Dei laxe appellari possunt. De primo et altero gradu habetur Act. 17.v.28. Quarta vero per excellentiam regeneratio fidelium, quae aeternae vitae principium est, hic nominatur vita Dei, quia tum proprie vivit Deus in nobis, et nos fruimur ejus vita, cum spiritu suo nos gubernat, juxta illud Rom. 8.10.11.12.13.14. Si Christus in vobis est, corpus quidem mortuum propter peccatum: Spiritus autem vita propter justitiam. Sed si Spiritus ejus qui excitavit Jesum a mortuis habitat in vobis, Is qui excitavit Christum ex mortuis, vivificabit etiam mortalia corpora vestra per inhabitantem ejus Spiritum in vobis. Nempe igitur, fratres, debitores sumus, non carni, ut secundum carnem vivamus. Nam si secundum carnem vixeritis, futurum est ut moriamini: sed si spiritu actiones corporis mortificetis, vivetis. Quotquot enim spiritu DEI ducuntur, ii sunt filii DEI.
english: X. What is the END of sacred theology? 1. The end of sacred theology is considered as twofold, internal and external. The internal is to teach the sacred mysteries and dogmas from the Scriptures — that is, to explain, demonstrate, and defend them rightly — unto exciting the life of God in the hearers. The external is the life of God, by which we are united, subjected, and obedient to our creator, redeemer, and sanctifier in light ([[Ephesians 4:17 >> Bible:Ephesians 4:17]]–18), or human beatitude begun, which is of faith, then consummated, which is of vision or eternal life, by which it is well with us in the way and in the fatherland in God, and by him we are nourished, strengthened, and refreshed as by our last real personal end ([[Genesis 15:1 >> Bible:Genesis 15:1]]).

2. This life, one and the same as to essence, remains from its beginning unto eternity ([[John 3:36 >> Bible:John 3:36]]; [[John 5:24 >> Bible:John 5:24]]; [[1 John 3:15 >> Bible:1 John 3:15]]). 3. And to live to God and to Christ ([[Romans 6:10 >> Bible:Romans 6:10]]–11) and to righteousness ([[1 Peter 2:24 >> Bible:1 Peter 2:24]]) is to direct all our actions and operations of faith and of life according to God's will unto God's glory, and to serve him in them, God himself acting within. 4. So we are said to live according to the flesh ([[Romans 8:12 >> Bible:Romans 8:12]]–13) — that is, to institute and carry out all our actions at the pleasure of original malice. Contrary to this is to live by the Spirit ([[Galatians 5:25 >> Bible:Galatians 5:25]]), to live justly, soberly, piously ([[Titus 2:12 >> Bible:Titus 2:12]]), no longer to live the remaining time in the flesh to human lusts but to the will of God, and to live according to God, that is, by the Spirit ([[1 Peter 4:2 >> Bible:1 Peter 4:2]], 6). So Paul ([[Galatians 2:19 >> Bible:Galatians 2:19]]–20): that I may live to God, he says, I have been crucified together with Christ — that is, I have been mortified, or my old Adam has been slain and a new one founded in me, that thereafter I may serve God by the Spirit of newness ([[2 Corinthians 4:10 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 4:10]]; [[Philippians 1:20 >> Bible:Philippians 1:20]]).

5. The life of GOD — not that by which God himself lives, who is life itself, but that by which we are made alive by him, or rather live — can be taken twofold ([[Ephesians 4:18 >> Bible:Ephesians 4:18]]): either that which is counted before God, as the glory of God ([[John 12:43 >> Bible:John 12:43]]), the righteousness of God ([[Romans 10:3 >> Bible:Romans 10:3]]–4, 6) by the grace of evangelical justification; or that which God communicates to us by the spirit of regeneration. 6. Whichever way you take it, the sense is the same. For this common life by which we are human beings, compared to the life of God, is nothing other than an empty image of life, not only because it quickly passes, but also because our souls are dead while living when they do not cling to God.

7. And there occur in this world four grades of life. For one is most common, which consists only in vigor, which belongs also to plants and the vegetable kingdom and by the Paracelsists is stretched also to the mineral kingdom. Another is universal, which consists in motion and sense, of which beasts also are partakers — which Thomas Campanella in his books on the sense of things extends to all parts of the world and the particles of parts. The third is human, by which we are sons of Adam. But the fourth is supernatural, which the faithful alone obtain. 8. All these grades of life are from God, and therefore can loosely be called the life of God. Of the first and second grade there is ([[Acts 17:28 >> Bible:Acts 17:28]]). But the fourth by excellence — the regeneration of the faithful, which is the principle of eternal life — is here named the life of God, because then God properly lives in us, and we enjoy his life, when he governs us by his Spirit, according to that ([[Romans 8:10 >> Bible:Romans 8:10]]–14): If Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the Spirit is life because of righteousness. But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also make alive your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you. Therefore, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, it will be that you die: but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are sons of God.

source_text:
Quanamobrem sacra dicitur? Quia ut arcana seorsum distinguitur a profana, eaque sive naturali quae sub lumine rectae rationis cognoscitur, et est pars verae philosophiae: sive superstitiosa, quae ex humanae rationis caecitate atque hallucinatione nascitur, et est pars falso nominatae scientiae, et inanis deceptionis, 1. Tim. 6.20. Col. 2.

An sit habitus intellectus practicus? Habitum intellectus esse nemo facile negaverit qui saltem eam sive doctrinam sive disciplinam agnoverit: an vero sit habitus practicus, diversae sunt Theologorum opiniones, tum veterum, tum recentium. Ideo autem peiusimum, id inepte et minus Theologice disputant scholae pontificiae; etsi non sine acumine et argutiis; qui philosophicas disputationes praesupponunt et postea de accommodatione Theologiae laborant: cumque scripturam non habeant comitem.

Ex recentioribus plerique mediam sententiam sequuntur, quidam primam, praecipui vero et antesignani ultimam amplecti videntur; argumento ordinis analytici quo Theologiam tractant, ut Melanchthon, Lutherus, Calvinus, Bullingerus, Ursinus, Keckermannus et nuper Guilielmus Amesius Anglus, professor Franequeranus, Doctor Constantinus L Empereur, professor Leidensis et alii. Cui postremae sententiae sic calculum nostrum adjicimus, ut primo terminos explicemus, deinde rationibus eam confirmemus. Termini sunt 1. Theologia; 2. habitus practicus; 3. praxis. Theologiam hic non intelligimus, quatenus est ipsius DEI, ut patet ex quaest. 1., sed quatenus nobis de regno DEI praescripta est. Habitus vero practicus dicitur denominative sicut et ipse intellectus, propter extensionem ad praxin.

Ita probamus. Primum, manifestis scripturae testimoniis; ultimum finem et Euangelii (de doctrina legis nullum est dubium quin practica sit) et systematis, quo doctrina Euangelii summatim et methodice disposita traditur, exprimentibus, Joh. 20.31. Rom. 15.4. 2. Tim. 3.16.17. Eccles. 12.13. 1. Tim. 1.5. 1. Cor. 8.1-3. et 13.2. Jac. 1.22.25. Apoc. 22.14.

Secundo, ex prima intentione et fine interno quae reapse idem sunt. Ea disciplina, cujus intentio prima et ultimus finis internus est practicus, est habitus practicus. Atqui sacrae Theologiae prima intentio et ultimus finis internus est practicus. Ergo sacra Theologia est habitus practicus. Major manifesta est. Minor probatur primo ex ratione prima quia ex testimoniis recitatis liquet, eam intendere fidem; quae per charitatem efficax est, Gal. 5.6. et fructus bonorum operum producit; quae conformia sint legi divinae in cultu DEI et amore proximi.

Deinde etiam Theologiam intendere ac respicere generationem et confirmationem fidei, et emendationem vitae ut fructum fidei, probatur ab ultimo fine externo, vitam nimirum aeternam, ad quam non nisi per fidem, tanquam medium apprehensivum, pervenire possumus. Is actus per quem solum homo ad vitam aeternam perducitur, primo intenditur a Theologia. Atqui fides est actus ille, per quem solum homo ad vitam aeternam perducitur, ut inferius suo loco probabitur. Ergo fides primo intenditur a Theologia.
english: Why is it called sacred? Because as something set apart it is distinguished from the profane — whether from natural theology, which is known under the light of right reason and is a part of true philosophy, or from the superstitious, which is born from the blindness and hallucination of human reason and is a part of falsely so-called knowledge and empty deceit ([[1 Timothy 6:20 >> Bible:1 Timothy 6:20]]; [[Colossians 2:8 >> Bible:Colossians 2:8]]).

Is it a practical habit of the intellect? That it is a habit of the intellect no one will easily deny who at least acknowledges it as a doctrine or discipline. But whether it is a practical habit, the opinions of theologians differ, both of the older and of the more recent. And it is worst of all that the papal schools dispute this ineptly and less theologically — though not without sharpness and subtleties — presupposing philosophical disputations and afterward laboring over the accommodation of theology, while they do not have Scripture as companion.

Among the more recent, most follow a middle opinion, some the first, but the chief and leading men seem to embrace the last, by the argument of the analytic order in which they treat theology — as Melanchthon, Luther, Calvin, Bullinger, Ursinus, Keckermann, and lately William Ames the Englishman, professor at Franeker, Dr. Constantijn L'Empereur, professor at Leiden, and others. To this last opinion we cast our vote in this way: first we explain the terms, then we confirm it by reasons. The terms are (1) theology, (2) practical habit, (3) practice. By theology here we do not understand that which is God's own, as is plain from question 1, but that which is prescribed to us concerning the kingdom of God. And a practical habit is so called denominatively, as the intellect itself is, because of its extension to practice.

So we prove it. First, by clear testimonies of Scripture that express the final end both of the Gospel (concerning the doctrine of the law there is no doubt that it is practical) and of the system in which the doctrine of the Gospel is handed down summarily and methodically arranged: ([[John 20:31 >> Bible:John 20:31]]; [[Romans 15:4 >> Bible:Romans 15:4]]; [[2 Timothy 3:16-17 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16-17]]; [[Ecclesiastes 12:13 >> Bible:Ecclesiastes 12:13]]; [[1 Timothy 1:5 >> Bible:1 Timothy 1:5]]; [[1 Corinthians 8:1-3 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 8:1-3]]; [[1 Corinthians 13:2 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 13:2]]; [[James 1:22-25 >> Bible:James 1:22-25]]; [[Revelation 22:14 >> Bible:Revelation 22:14]]).

Second, from the first intention and the internal end, which in reality are the same. That discipline whose first intention and last internal end is practical is a practical habit. But the first intention and last internal end of sacred theology is practical. Therefore sacred theology is a practical habit. The major is plain. The minor is proved first from the first reason, because from the testimonies recited it is clear that theology aims at faith, which is effective through love ([[Galatians 5:6 >> Bible:Galatians 5:6]]) and produces the fruit of good works that conform to the divine law in the worship of God and the love of neighbor.

Next, that theology also aims at and regards the generation and confirmation of faith, and the amendment of life as the fruit of faith, is proved from the last external end — namely eternal life — to which we can come only through faith as the apprehending means. That act by which alone a person is led to eternal life is first intended by theology. But faith is that act by which alone a person is led to eternal life, as will be proved below in its place. Therefore faith is first intended by theology.

source_text: 13. Nos respondemus ad primum, primo, nondum liquere, an illa loca de sacra Theologia, ut disciplina methodice conformata ac disposita, de qua quaestio hic est, agant, atque ita dubium per aeque dubium probari. Secundo, si liberaliter concedamus, haec et alia dicta scripturae, quae in hanc rem allegantur, de sacra theologia, ut tali, agere; tamen is haud efficiunt non practicam, sed theoreticam, aut saltem partim theoreticam partim practicam, quorum alterutrum, qui a nobis seorsim sentiunt, obtinere cupiunt. Nam ipsa illa loca accuratius inspecta Hebraismum ostendunt, quo sapiens pro prudente et justo in scripturis frequentatur, quia is e justis actionibus fere ubique describitur. Sic et totus liber proverbiorum voce sapientia passim utitur. Ex cap. 10.v.11. inquit doctissimus Thomas Cartwrightus in hunc locum, apparet, eum justum appellari, qui hic appellatur sapiens, ut pro sapiente vere habendus non sit, qui fide justificatus justitiam non colit. Verum enimvero utramque hoc ad quidem nonnulla documenta in Theologia, quae in se ac per se quidem considerata, sint theoremata rerum, quae iis cognoscendae proponuntur: at, ut aequum est, ad suum totum tanquam partes theologiae, et ad hujus ultimum finem relata et aestimata, omnia esse theoremata morum sive practica monumenta, quippe quae traduntur, non ut sciantur solummodo aut contemplentur, sed ut ad cultum Dei et salutem hominis referantur, unde et insigni Dei rerumque divinarum scientia theoretica nihilo meliores aut beatiores redduntur hypocritae et impii. Vere enim Justinus Martyr: religionis nostrae non in verbis, sed in factis. Quo respectu neglecto et insuper habito nulla prorsus disciplina practica dabitur, quia nulla praxis est, quae non includat aliquam notitiam. 14. Distinguimus in primo syllogismo majorem. Nam objectum disciplinae practicae est τὸ πρακτόν, vel in se et natura sua, vel in alio, quod etsi distinctum est ab objecto, tamen ita ei conjungitur, ut propter id objectum cognoscatur et disciplina tractetur. Cum hac vero distinctione minor vera non est. Nam etsi Deus in se et natura sua non sit τὸ πρακτόν, tamen finis simpliciter primus et necessarius, et justificatio nominis ejus, propter quam in theologia cognoscendus proponitur, est τὸ πρακτόν. Johannes Duns Scotus in 1. Sent. q.4. ubi et has propositiones theologicas, Deus est trinus, Pater generat Filium, Pater et Filius spirant Spiritum sanctum, asserit esse practicas: quia includunt virtualiter notitiam rectitudinis dilectionis in tres Deitatis personas, nulla exclusa, tendentis. Quod vero ad res divinas, vel sint a solo Deo, ut opera creationis et redemptionis, vel principaliter a Deo, et secundario certoque respectu, ab homine quoque, quatenus hominis actiones etiam ad eas concurrunt, ut fides, justificatio, sanctificatio, totusque Dei cultus. Priores ad τὸ πρακτόν eum in modum referuntur, quo Deus: posteriores vero in se et natura sua sunt talia.
english: 13. We reply to the first. First, it is not yet clear whether those places treat of sacred theology as a discipline methodically shaped and arranged — which is the question here — and so a doubt is proved by an equally doubtful thing. Second, even if we liberally grant that these and other sayings of Scripture alleged for this matter treat of sacred theology as such, they still do not prove it non-practical but theoretical, or at least partly theoretical and partly practical — which is what those who differ from us separately desire. For those places more carefully inspected show a Hebraism by which wise is frequently used in Scripture for the prudent and the just, because he is described almost everywhere from just actions. So also the whole book of Proverbs uses the word wisdom everywhere. From chapter 10 verse 11 the most learned Thomas Cartwright says on this place that he who is here called wise appears to be called just, so that he who, justified by faith, does not cultivate righteousness is not truly to be counted wise.

Yet in truth, even if some documents in theology, considered in themselves and by themselves, are theorems of things proposed to be known: still, when related and weighed, as is fair, to their whole as parts of theology and to its last end, all are theorems of manners or practical monuments — for they are handed down not only to be known or contemplated, but to be referred to the worship of God and the salvation of man. Hence by a notable theoretical science of God and divine things hypocrites and the ungodly are made no better or happier. Truly Justin Martyr: our religion consists not in words but in deeds. If that respect is neglected and set aside, no practical discipline at all will be given, because there is no practice that does not include some knowledge.

14. In the first syllogism we distinguish the major. For the object of a practical discipline is the doable (τὸ πρακτόν), either in itself and its nature, or in another which, though distinct from the object, is so joined to it that the object is known and the discipline treated for its sake. With this distinction the minor is not true. For although God in himself and his nature is not the doable, yet the simply first and necessary end, and the justification of his name, for which he is proposed to be known in theology, is the doable. John Duns Scotus (on the Sentences book 1 question 4) asserts that even these theological propositions — God is triune; the Father begets the Son; the Father and the Son breathe the Holy Spirit — are practical, because they virtually include the knowledge of the rightness of love tending to the three persons of the Deity, none excluded. As for divine things, some are from God alone, as the works of creation and redemption; others principally from God and secondarily, in a certain respect, also from man, insofar as human actions also concur toward them — as faith, justification, sanctification, and the whole worship of God. The former are referred to the doable in the way God is; the latter are such in themselves and their nature.

source_text: 15. Ad tertium, Negamus consequentiam, quia non quavis cognitio facit disciplinam theoreticam, sed ea duntaxat, quae ad praxin per se non dirigit. Atqui Theologica Dei cognitio hominem ad praxin pietatis per se dirigit. 16. Ad quartum, consequentiam negamus. Consistit aeterna vita in cognitione non tanquam fine, sed tanquam in medio ad finem, sine quo finem nemo adultus assequitur, nimirum salutem suam et sanctificationem nominis Dei. Adstipulatur nobis inter plures D. Johannes Gerhardus professor Jenensis praefat. Meditationum. Constat, inquiens, Theologiam esse doctrinam practicam, ac proinde minus recte eos sentire, qui speculativam eam esse contendunt, quo in numero sunt quidam ex scholasticis. Quamvis enim non solum agenda, sed etiam credenda et speranda in hac coelesti philosophia proponantur, id tamen non impedit, quo minus practica adhuc dicatur. Nam et Medicina in quorundam theoria occupata est, nec tamen propterea Theorica disciplina est, quia hanc ipsam theoriam, praxeos ratione, ac in ordine ad praxin sectatur: perinde se res habet in Theologia. Ut jam non addam, in illis ipsis credendis, sive in fidei articulis, non nudam notitiam, sed et assensum requiri, quem ex parte voluntatis actum esse, argumentis confirmant illi, ad quos haec cura pertinet. Quod si Theologia est doctrina practica, utique etiam finis ejus non erit nuda gnosis, et subtilis theoria, sed potius praxis. Haec si sciveritis, beati estis, si feceritis ea, dicit Salvator ad discipulos. Non in verbis, sed in factis, vires nostrae religionis consistunt, dicit Justinus. Summa religionis est, imitari eum, quem colis, dicit Augustinus. Quodsi ergo Christianae religionis finis ac perfectio, non est nuda gnosis, sed praxis, quam paucos hodie invenies vere Christianos! Multum ubique scientiae, conscientiae parum. Rectissime fit, quod orthodoxia libris, disputationibus, concionibus, et modis omnibus defenditur: sed et vita professioni Christianae ut respondeat, opera danda. Haec D. Gerhardus.
english: 15. To the third, we deny the consequence, because not just any cognition makes a theoretical discipline, but only that which does not of itself direct to practice. But the theological knowledge of God of itself directs a person to the practice of piety.

16. To the fourth, we deny the consequence. Eternal life consists in cognition not as in an end, but as in a means to the end, without which no adult attains the end — namely his salvation and the sanctification of God's name. Doctor Johannes Gerhard, professor at Jena, agrees with us among others in the preface to his Meditations. It is agreed, he says, that theology is a practical doctrine, and therefore those think less rightly who contend that it is speculative, among whom are some of the scholastics. For although not only things to be done, but also things to be believed and hoped, are proposed in this heavenly philosophy, that still does not hinder its still being called practical. For medicine too is occupied with the theory of certain things, and yet is not therefore a theoretical discipline, because it pursues that very theory by reason of practice and in order to practice: the matter stands likewise in theology. Not to add already that in those very things to be believed, or in the articles of faith, not bare knowledge but also assent is required, which those to whom this care belongs confirm by arguments to be an act on the will's side. But if theology is a practical doctrine, then surely its end also will not be bare knowledge and subtle theory, but rather practice. If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them, says the Savior to the disciples. The strength of our religion consists not in words but in deeds, says Justin. The sum of religion is to imitate him whom you worship, says Augustine. If therefore the end and perfection of the Christian religion is not bare knowledge but practice, how few will you find today who are truly Christians! Everywhere much science, little conscience. It is most right that orthodoxy is defended by books, disputations, sermons, and every means: but care must also be taken that life answer to the Christian profession. Thus Doctor Gerhard.
